card.hook: Look above the door and you'll spot the old 'Frick & Lindsay Co' lettering, a leftover from the days when this grand Beaux-Arts front belonged to an industrial warehouse. Now it's home to one of the world's most famous pop artists.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Sandusky Street and General Robinson Street, across the street from the front. The middle of the building is about 35 m to the south-west, so face south-west and tilt up at the entrance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x from across the street. If you can't step back far enough to fit the whole front in, switch to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for a closer shot of the lettering above the door.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the facade with the vertical lines, so the building doesn't lean backwards when you tilt your phone up.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon on a clear day is a good bet, when the front is evenly lit and not in harsh glare. Street shadows can fall across the facade, so take a quick look when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Try the museum front on Sandusky Street, next to the big silver Brillo box if it's out there when you arrive. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x if you want more in, and keep the museum facade behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the museum, still photos are fine but flash and selfie sticks aren't allowed. Photo rules can differ in special exhibitions, so check the official site before you go in.
card.challenge: Get the 'Frick & Lindsay Co' lettering and the entrance in one straight, centred shot, with no leaning walls and no cars in the corners.
card.good_to_know: Andy Warhol was born in Pittsburgh, and this museum holds the largest collection in North America devoted to a single artist. It has seven floors and 17 galleries, and it's one of the four Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh. It opened in May 1994, and about 25,000 people turned up in its first weekend.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the corner of Sandusky Street and General Robinson Street, across the street from the front. The middle of the building is about 35 m to the south-west, so face south-west and tilt up at the entrance.

card.hook: Picture a baseball stadium with a river at its feet, a bright yellow bridge beside it and the Downtown skyline close by. That's PNC Park, and you barely have to try to make it look good.
card.stand_here: Stand in Allegheny Landing on the riverfront side, with the stadium ahead of you. The Clemente Bridge and the other yellow bridges should sit close by in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the stadium and the yellow bridges into one shot. Then try 1x for a cleaner, less stretched ballpark, and 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines, put the river edge or railing on a lower line to keep the horizon level, and leave some water in front so the stadium doesn't look flat.
card.best_time: Golden hour is lovely here. After a game is good too, when the riverfront is quieter.
card.selfie_here: Take a selfie at the Roberto Clemente statue just outside the park gates, a few steps from the bridge end. Use the front camera and hold it a little low so the statue fits behind you. For a second one, try mid-span on the yellow bridge with the view over your shoulder, and check on site what ends up behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the Roberto Clemente Bridge to look back toward the stadium while you stand in front of the ballpark.
card.rules_and_safety: The Roberto Clemente Bridge is closed to vehicles on game days but stays open to walkers, so check it's open to pedestrians before you set off. Check the official site for access to PNC Park itself.
card.challenge: Find a spot where the yellow bridge and the stadium both fit in your shot with the horizon dead level. Gridlines are your friend.
card.good_to_know: PNC Park opened during the 2001 season, and it's built with steel and limestone instead of brick bases. Its arches and steel trusswork echo classic ballparks like Pittsburgh's own Forbes Field. It seats 38,747 people, yet it still looks compact from across the water. The bridge is named for Pirates player Roberto Clemente.

card.hook: Sixty-eight thousand seats is a lot of building to squeeze into one phone screen. The trick is to stop trying to fit it all in and let one big flight of steps and a scoreboard tell the story.
card.stand_here: Stand at the steps up to Gate A under the main scoreboard, on the south side of Acrisure Stadium. It's a short walk from the centre of the stadium toward the river side. Face the steps and scoreboard, and keep the river behind you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a person on the steps with the scoreboard behind them. If you're close and the building won't fit, drop to 0.5x. Save 2x or more for details, like the statue near Gate A.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the stadium front level, then tap your friend's face and slide it a touch darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the scoreboard.
card.best_time: Check the home-game fixtures before you go, because the steps can fill with fans. Visitor guides rate golden hour for the bridge view, and you can judge the light on your own screen when you get there.
card.selfie_here: Walk to the middle of the Roberto Clemente Bridge and face back toward the stadium, with the skyline and PNC Park on either side. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the stadium over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are typically not allowed inside the stadium, according to a third-party visitor site. The steps and exterior are outside, but the inside is for ticketed events, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get a friend on the steps with the scoreboard sitting just above their head, then see if you can find the Pitt Panther statue for your detail shot.
card.good_to_know: Acrisure Stadium is still often called Heinz Field, and it opened in 2001. It's home to the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Pittsburgh Panthers, and it uses about 12,000 tons of steel as a nod to the city's steel history. Near Gate A, the Panther statue stands over a paved picture of the Cathedral of Learning.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the steps up to Gate A under the main scoreboard, on the south side of Acrisure Stadium. It's a short walk from the centre of the stadium toward the river side. Face the steps and scoreboard, and keep the river behind you.

card.hook: Pittsburgh doesn't hide up here. The skyline, three rivers and a row of bridges are all laid out below the rail, like the city is showing off.
card.stand_here: Stand at the fenced lookout on Grandview Avenue (136-160 Grandview Ave) on Mount Washington. Face across the rivers toward Downtown.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole skyline, rivers and bridges in one shot. Try 0.5x for more of the rail and the sweep of the valley. Then go to 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the bridges or one cluster of towers.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, so the skyline and rivers sit in neat bands.
card.best_time: Sunset and the half hour after it are the best light, when the city lights start to come on. Stay a bit longer and try night mode on the lit-up skyline.
card.selfie_here: If the main platform is packed, try the Thomas J. Gallagher Overlook at the corner of Grandview Avenue and Bertha Street. One guide calls it a quieter spot with nearly the same view. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the skyline over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Parking can be scarce at weekends and in the evenings, and there may be no restrooms at the overlook, so plan ahead. Check the official site before you go for any local restrictions.
card.challenge: Take one photo with the rail in the corner and one without. Which one makes the city look further away?
card.good_to_know: This hill was once called Coal Hill, because coal was mined and stone quarried here. By 1876 it was Mount Washington, and a year later the view of the city was first drawn from up here. Lots of the Pittsburgh skyline photos you've seen were taken from this hill.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the fenced lookout on Grandview Avenue (136-160 Grandview Ave) on Mount Washington. Face across the rivers toward Downtown.

card.hook: Picture 42 storeys of pointy Gothic limestone looming over a student campus, then hearing everyone call it "Cathy". That's the Cathedral of Learning, and it's much bigger in person than you expect.
card.stand_here: Stand in Schenley Plaza in Oakland and face the tower across the open paved space. For a view with Heinz Chapel and the Stephen Foster Memorial beside it, try the southwest corner of the plaza.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole tower in, then switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look. Turn on gridlines, keep the phone level, and line the tower up with a vertical line so the sides stay straight. If your phone has 2x or 5x, save it for the stonework and the glowing top.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or the pale stone, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the limestone doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Mid-morning to afternoon on a clear day lights the side of the tower facing the plaza. Dusk is great too if the golden lights near the top are on. Switch on night mode and hold still for a moment.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Mary Schenley Memorial Fountain, across from Schenley Plaza and in front of the Frick Fine Arts Building. Turn so the Cathedral is behind you, use the front camera (try 0.5x), and hold the phone low and tilted up so the tower fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Schenley Plaza, across Forbes Avenue from the Cathedral, and shoot upward against the sky while you pose with the tower behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The tower's inside is a working university building, so check the official site before you go if you want to head in.
card.challenge: Get the whole tower in one shot with a tree or a few passers-by in front for scale, and keep both sides dead straight.
card.good_to_know: The tower rises 42 storeys, 535 feet (163 m), and is clad in Indiana limestone. It was commissioned in 1921, its exterior was finished in 1934, and it was dedicated in 1937. The top floors have golden lights that are switched on after Pitt football wins and other victories, so the crown can glow amber.

card.hook: On Pirates game days this bridge shuts to cars and turns into one big footpath to the ballpark, with a river and a city skyline behind it. It's a busy, car-free spot, and those towers and cables make a great picture.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Roberto Clemente Bridge, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Face north-west and keep the bridge in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x so both towers and the sweep of the cables fit in one frame. Switch to 1x for a natural view of the deck and one tower, then try 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) for the eye-bars and hangers.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the bridge, then drag the brightness slider down a touch so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Evening is lovely, once the bridge lights are on and the structure glows against the dusk sky. Daytime is better for clean, crisp views of the metalwork. Expect crowds on Pirates game days.
card.selfie_here: Try the North Shore Riverwalk, on the path midway between the Roberto Clemente and Andy Warhol bridges. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the city skyline and a yellow bridge sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the North Shore riverbank on the Three Rivers Heritage Trail, so the bridge shows from the side with city buildings behind you (there's no exact point, so just pick a clear bit of path).
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photos on the bridge are fine, but commercial photography or filming may need permits. Don't block the path while you shoot, and stay aware of your surroundings if you're on the bridge late at night.
card.challenge: Line up the deck with a gridline so it looks perfectly straight, then find the Clemente statue near the stadium end for a bonus shot.
card.good_to_know: The Roberto Clemente Bridge, also called the Sixth Street Bridge, opened on 29 September 1928. It was renamed in 1998 after Pirates player Roberto Clemente. It's one of the Three Sisters, the only trio of near-twin suspension bridges of their kind in the United States, and it was first lit on 20 November 2002.

card.hook: Most people ride a little wooden car up Mount Washington and shoot from the deck. Walk a bit further and you get the whole city with hardly any fencing across it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Grandview Avenue near the Point of View statue, a short walk uphill from the upper station. Face out over the city and the rivers spread below you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the full skyline and rivers, then try 1x for a more natural look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the incline, a bridge or a single building.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, then tap the skyline and slide it a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk usually works well, when the light is softer and the city lights start to come on. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall to keep things steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the fenced observation platform just outside the upper station, on Grandview Avenue. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone offers it) and stand with the station behind you; there's room to take your time posing.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand in the free parking area across West Carson Street from the lower station (1197 W. Carson St.) so the whole station fits, while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is generally allowed at the Duquesne Incline, but professional or commercial shoots may need special arrangements. The official viewing deck is reached by riding the incline, so check the official site for fares, hours and closures before you go.
card.challenge: Get a skyline shot with no railing across it, then ride up and get one with the red incline cars in front. Which do you like better?
card.good_to_know: The Duquesne Incline opened in 1877 and was designed by Pittsburgh engineer Samuel Diescher. The track climbs about 122 metres (400 feet) at a 30-degree angle. It closed in 1962, local residents raised the money to restore it, and it reopened in 1963; it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975.

card.hook: Cross Schenley Drive, climb up onto the hill, and there's a whole Victorian glasshouse at the far end of the lawn, posing like it knows you've got a camera.
card.stand_here: Stand on Flagstaff Hill, the hilltop across Schenley Drive from the main entrance. Face back across the lawn and trees toward the conservatory's front.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the front framed by lawn and trees. If you're standing closer and want the whole building plus the stairs, try 0.5x, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the dome and glasswork.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the building along the upper third, with lawn or trees filling the bottom, then tap the glass and drag the slider a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the front.
card.best_time: Autumn is lovely here because the trees around the hill turn colourful. On any day, softer morning or late-afternoon light tends to suit glass and brick, and late afternoon is also kinder for selfies by the fountain.
card.selfie_here: Stand by the copper fountain in front of Botany Hall, with its stone stairs and wood doors behind you, and use the front camera. For another backdrop, climb the double curved stairs at the main entrance and let the glass front fill the space over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Flagstaff Hill's stone wall and steps, across the street from the main entrance, and frame the whole building with you in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are fine outside, but not in the gated outdoor gardens, and going inside or taking indoor photos needs arranging, so check the official Phipps site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three frames from the hill with different amounts of sky, then pick the one where the glass looks like it's floating above the lawn.
card.good_to_know: Henry Phipps Jr. gave Phipps Conservatory to the city in 1893, and it opened to the public on 7 December that year. Lord & Burnham designed the glass and metalwork, and it's still counted as a fine example of Victorian greenhouse building. A newer Welcome Center with a neo-Victorian dome was added in 2005, so old and new sit side by side.

card.hook: This building is roughly 217 m across, so it will not fit in one frame from close up, and that's fine. Your job is to pick the bit you love: the whole frontage, a slice of stonework, or a tiny you at the door.
card.stand_here: Head to the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Oakland, where the phone icon on the map sits right at the building itself. Face the frontage, then step back as far as the pavement allows to fit more in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more of that long building, then try 1x for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. Go to 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for carved stonework and entrance details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines and line the edges of the building up with them so the vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: A dry day in daylight suits the outside best. Early morning tends to be quieter if you want fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the Dippy the Diplodocus replica outside on Forbes Avenue, so the stone facade is behind you and you both fit in one frame. Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold your phone a bit higher and let the dinosaur and building sneak in over your shoulder. The front entrance steps up to the bronze doors make a good backup spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the galleries, selfie sticks aren't allowed, and you need to stay at least two feet away from specimens when taking photos or selfies. It's worth checking with the museum about photography before you start snapping indoors.
card.challenge: Get Dippy and you in the same frame, then take a second shot where you look as small as a dinosaur snack.
card.good_to_know: Andrew Carnegie, the Pittsburgh industrialist, founded the museum in 1896. Its scientists unearthed the fossils of Diplodocus carnegii in 1899, and the collection includes the world's first specimen of a Tyrannosaurus rex. The museum holds about 22 million specimens, with around 10,000 on view at any one time.

card.hook: From up on Mount Washington, Pittsburgh's rivers look like they're being introduced to each other, and the park sits in the middle like a green wedge of cheese. Two rivers meet, become the Ohio, and you get the whole story in one frame.
card.stand_here: Head to the Mount Washington overlook on Grandview Avenue and face north-east. The park and its fountain will be right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to fit in the park, both rivers and the bridges. Then try 1x for a neater frame of the Point, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the fountain or a single bridge.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines and put the fountain near a crossing point, with a strip of park along the bottom so the Point looks like a wedge of land.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to evening is lovely, when the light falls on the park and the bridges. Dusk works too, when the fountain is lit, so try night mode and hold your phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Walk down to the tip of the Point by the fountain basin, at water level, and put the fountain at your back with a river on each side. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze it all in, and keep the fountain over your shoulder (a travel guide calls it one of the most photographed spots in Pittsburgh).
card.ask_someone: Ask someone on the Great Lawn to shoot across the grass toward the fountain, with you standing in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: There are no guardrails near the riverbanks, so stay back from the edge and keep your phone and belongings secure.
card.challenge: Can you get both rivers and the Fort Duquesne Bridge's steel arch in one shot, then zoom in until the arch frames the stadiums across the Allegheny?
card.good_to_know: The park covers 36 acres and opened in August 1974, once its fountain was finished. It also marks the outlines of Fort Pitt and Fort Duquesne. The little brick Blockhouse from 1764 is believed to be the oldest building in Western Pennsylvania. The fountain seems to run from roughly spring to October, so check before you go if it matters to your picture.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Mount Washington overlook on Grandview Avenue and face north-east. The park and its fountain will be right in front of you.

card.hook: At first glance it looks like a very long, very plain old warehouse, and that's exactly why it makes such a good phone photo. All those straight lines and rows of windows give you a clean, simple subject.
card.stand_here: Stand at the corner of Smallman Street and 13th Street, at the building's 13th Street end. Face along the Smallman Street front, which stretches away from you along the pavement to the south-west.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole long front into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or higher (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the windows and wall texture.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the roofline and window rows up with them, then keep your phone level so the walls don't lean in.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, when the outside looks best. A weekday morning is usually quieter, so you'll get fewer people and vehicles in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Head to the giant Heinz ketchup bottle on Smallman Street near 12th Street and stand under the bottle's platform. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and let the museum's brick facade rise behind your shoulder. The bottle's position was reported a few years ago, so it's worth a quick look on site that it's still there.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the museum, personal phone photos are generally allowed, but flash is often restricted, so look out for signs. The museum is ticketed, so check the official site for visiting details before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole front, then one close-up of a single window, and see if friends can match the close-up to the building.
card.good_to_know: This is the largest history museum in Pennsylvania, and it's a Smithsonian affiliate. The building is a century-old warehouse that was once the Chautauqua Lake Ice Company building, and the museum opened there in 1996. A Smithsonian wing was added in 2004, and there are six floors of exhibitions inside.

card.hook: Smallman Street does something rare: it runs dead straight away from you, all the way to an old railroad produce terminal, with the city piled up behind it. Your photo practically composes itself.
card.stand_here: Stand on Smallman Street in front of St. Stanislaus Church. Face down the street toward the old Pennsylvania Railroad Produce Terminal at the far end.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the street, the terminal and the city all fit in one frame. Then try 2x (or more, depending on your phone) to pull the far end of the street closer. On Penn Avenue or at Doughboy Square, switch to 0.5x to get the skyline and the foreground together.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the street's centre line on the middle vertical line, so the street leads the eye straight to the terminal.
card.best_time: Go around sunrise or sunset. The low light throws long shadows along the street and adds depth. If you can, skip Saturdays, because the Strip gets very busy then.
card.selfie_here: Sit on the benches in front of the wall mural at the Strip District Terminal (2101 Smallman St), with the colourful steps nearby. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the mural in over your shoulder. For a bolder, close-up backdrop, the red, purple and pink stairs in the 17th Street passageway (1698 Smallman St) work well.
card.ask_someone: On the 16th Street Bridge walkway (reached from Penn Avenue at 16th Street), ask someone to take your photo with the upriver view of the Strip District and the former Heinz factory behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep your phone steady against the traffic and watch for passing vehicles while you line up the shot. It's a public street, so check current conditions when you arrive.
card.challenge: Get the street's centre line perfectly on that middle grid line, then see if a passing car or person sneaks into the frame at just the right moment.
card.good_to_know: The Strip District is a whole neighbourhood, not a single building, so the street itself is the star. Smallman Street is a classic vantage point for it. If you've time for a second view, Doughboy Square has a World War I doughboy monument in the foreground, with the Strip and downtown spread out below.

card.hook: Here's the trick with PPG Place: the buildings are covered in mirror, so the sky and the rest of downtown end up in your photo too. It's a bit like a castle that got a glass makeover.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of the open-air plaza at PPG Place and look up at the glass towers. Tip your phone up and let the towers rise out of the corners of the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the tall towers and the plaza in one shot. Then try 1x for calmer reflections, and 2x or 5x (if your phone has them) to pick out the spires.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the tower edges close to straight, then tap a mid-bright patch of glass and slide it a little darker so the sky doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Golden hour is best for glowing reflections in the glass. In winter, mid-morning works nicely for the ice rink.
card.selfie_here: In warmer months, stand close to the fountain jets in the plaza, use the front camera at 0.5x and see if you can fit the towers behind you. In winter, take it at the ice rink with the towers behind you for a festive shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The plaza is open public space, but the winter ice rink and any events may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go. Rooftop views aren't open to the public, so stay at ground level.
card.challenge: Find a spot where a tower reflects another tower, then see if you can fit yourself into the mirror-within-a-mirror.
card.good_to_know: PPG Place is six glass buildings around a plaza, designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee as a modern take on neo-Gothic. It's covered in 19,750 pieces of mirrored glass and topped with 231 glass spires, and the tallest building, One PPG Place, has 40 storeys. It was dedicated on 11 April 1984.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of the open-air plaza at PPG Place and look up at the glass towers. Tip your phone up and let the towers rise out of the corners of the frame.

card.hook: Walk a few blocks here and you'll fill your camera roll with old theatre fronts, glowing signs and doorways, all without getting tired feet. It's a tiny stretch of Downtown Pittsburgh, and it's very good at making you look like you planned your day.
card.stand_here: Stand at Agnes R. Katz Plaza, about 100 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Pick a corner where you can see a theatre front along the street rather than straight on.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for street scenes and theatre fronts. Switch to 0.5x when a building is too tall or the pavement is too narrow to fit it in, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for signs, lettering and doorway details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and keep the buildings' vertical lines parallel to the screen edges, and step back instead of tilting the phone up so the buildings don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Early evening is lovely, when the lights and signs come on and the sky isn't completely dark yet. Daytime is better for clear, crisp pictures of the buildings.
card.selfie_here: Sit on one of the granite eye-shaped benches on the central terrace at Agnes R. Katz Plaza (Seventh Street and Penn Avenue corner), with the 25-foot bronze fountain behind you. Use the front camera and try 0.5x if your phone has it, so the fountain fits over your shoulder. The benches were expected to become photo landmarks, so you're in good company.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Penn Avenue sidewalk, facing into the plaza, while you sit on the eye-benches, so you and the fountain both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep an eye on traffic and other pedestrians when you step back to frame a shot. The theatres and galleries are separate venues, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or take photos indoors.
card.challenge: Collect the set: one wide street scene, one close-up of a single theatre front, and one tiny detail like lettering or a doorway, all within a couple of blocks.
card.good_to_know: The Cultural District covers fourteen square blocks and has six theatres, galleries, restaurants and shops. Heinz Hall began as the Loew's Penn Theatre in 1927 and became a concert hall in 1971, while the Benedum Center was the Stanley Theater, which opened in 1928. The district was H. J. Heinz II's idea, and the Pittsburgh Cultural Trust, formed in 1984, looks after it.

card.hook: Picture a 40-foot arched window glowing on a downtown street. This was nearly a car park. Heinz Hall's big curved front is the reason you'll want your phone out.
card.stand_here: Stand near 6th Street, right where the phone icon sits on the map, and face the front of Heinz Hall at 600 Penn Avenue. If you can't fit the whole front in, walk back along the pavement.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x, because you're close to the building. Switch to 1x for the doors and the lower part of the arch. If you step back, try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the top of the arched window.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the arched window, then slide it a little darker if the bright glass or sky washes out.
card.best_time: Evening is lovely, when the building is likely to be lit and people are arriving for a show. Daytime is quieter if you want a clear view of the front.
card.selfie_here: Head inside to the Grand Lobby and stand in front of one of the 15-foot chandeliers. Use the front camera, hold it a little above eye level, and let the ornate decor fill the background. Check with the venue before you take photos.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the pavement at the corner of Sixth Street and Penn Avenue, where the entrances face the street, and ask a passer-by to take your picture so the whole front of the building is in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos during performances are generally not allowed, but the lobby and architecture are usually fine before or after a show. Entry depends on events, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and get the edges of the arch running perfectly straight, with not a single stranger in the shot.
card.good_to_know: Heinz Hall opened in 1927 as Loew's Penn Theatre, a grand movie palace by the architects Rapp & Rapp. It closed in 1964 and was due to be demolished for a car park, but it was rescued and reopened as a concert hall on 10 September 1971. Today it's home to the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra, seats 2,676 people and puts on about 200 performances a year.

card.hook: Picture tidy mid-19th-century shopfronts standing right next to shiny glass towers, and you in the middle of it all with a coffee. That's Market Square, and one photo can hold the city's past and its present.
card.stand_here: Start at PPG Place, just to the south-west of Market Square, on the plaza among the glass towers. Face back across the plaza toward the square and let the glass buildings frame it.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x at PPG Place to fit the towers and the square into one frame. Switch to 1x once you're in the square for a natural view, then try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for umbrellas, shopfronts and people at the tables.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and hold your phone level so the towers stand straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: The square changes with the seasons, so pick what you'd like in your picture: umbrellas, the fountain, the ice rink or the holiday market. There's also a farmers' market on Thursdays and a Christmas village, so you'll never get quite the same photo twice.
card.selfie_here: Step into the open middle of Market Square and pose among the colorful umbrellas and patio chairs, with the surrounding buildings behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a little low so the buildings fit over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: One guide says there are police officers all over the Market Square area, so it feels very safe to visit. There may be construction at the square, so check for current work before you go.
card.challenge: Find a spot where a 19th-century frontage and a modern tower share the same frame, then get yourself into it with a big grin.
card.good_to_know: Market Square was laid out in 1784 and has been a meeting place ever since. It held the town's first courthouse and jail in 1795, and the first newspaper west of the Allegheny Mountains was printed here. A rebuild in 2009-2010 turned it into a European-style piazza with traffic moved to the edges, which is why it's now a place to linger.

card.hook: Picture three yellow bridges lined up along the river like siblings squeezing into a family photo. That's the Three Sisters, and the way they repeat one after another is what makes them so easy to photograph.
card.stand_here: Head to the railing in Fort Duquesne Boulevard Park, near the 7th Street end. Face west along the Allegheny toward the Roberto Clemente Bridge, with its sister bridges lined up beyond it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the whole row fits. Then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) to squeeze the bridges closer together. Use 0.5x only if you want the railing and river in the foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the Clemente Bridge along one of the lower lines, and keep your phone level so the bridge decks look straight.
card.best_time: The bridges are lit up, so an after-dark shot works well here. Switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep things steady.
card.selfie_here: Try Allegheny Landing Park on the North Shore, between the Clemente and Warhol bridges, where the city view falls between the two spans. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and angle yourself so the bridges and skyline slip into the frame. The bridges may not land right behind you, so check the preview and shuffle until it looks good.
card.ask_someone: On the PNC Park side, ask a passer-by to frame you so the Roberto Clemente Bridge and the city skyline both fit in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The Roberto Clemente Bridge is sometimes closed to vehicles on game days, and access can be restricted for events, so check before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get all three sisters in one frame, with the row of bridges leading your eye down the river?
card.good_to_know: The Three Sisters were built between 1924 and 1928, and they're the only trio of nearly identical bridges in the United States. They were also the country's first self-anchored suspension spans, with the steel chains fixed to the ends of the deck instead of to huge blocks on the river banks. That's what gives them such a light, tidy look.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the railing in Fort Duquesne Boulevard Park, near the 7th Street end. Face west along the Allegheny toward the Roberto Clemente Bridge, with its sister bridges lined up beyond it.

card.hook: Picture a wide river with sky, water and the far bank stacked one above the other, like a layer cake you can photograph. That's the whole charm of North Shore Riverfront Park, and there's plenty of room to take your time.
card.stand_here: Head for the spot near North Shore Trail and stand about 630 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Stop wherever the river view opens up and nobody's walking through your shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in all that open river and sky, then switch to 1x for a more natural view. Try 2x or 5x for details on the far bank or boats on the water (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, then tap the brightest part of the sky and slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and calmer water, which is great for reflections. Weekday mornings are likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the Water Steps in the park: use the front camera at 0.5x and stand on the sandstone blocks with the textured steps and the river edge behind you. Or head to the Mister Rogers statue (Tribute to Children) on North Shore Drive, where guides say selfies are common and the trail and skyline sit behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The Water Steps are only open at some times, so check before you go. A review warns that the historic WWII landing ship docked at the park has uneven surfaces, so watch your step. Paths and viewing areas can change with works or events, so check the official site for closures.
card.challenge: Find a railing or a tree branch to put in front of you, then see if the water is calm enough to give you a reflection too.
card.good_to_know: North Shore Riverfront Park is a riverside green space on Pittsburgh's North Shore, so the water is always right next to you. It's a nice place to slow down and take a few relaxed photos. Surfaces, paths and viewing areas can change with works or events, so check the official site before you head out.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the spot near North Shore Trail and stand about 630 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Stop wherever the river view opens up and nobody's walking through your shot.

card.hook: From up high, the Smithfield Street Bridge looks like a curved steel ribbon laid across the river, and it still reads clearly on a small phone screen. It's the shot that makes your camera roll look like you planned it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Mount Washington overlook on Grand View Avenue and face the bridge, looking down on it. You want the river and the approach into downtown in the frame too.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the bridge, river and downtown all fit. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the trusses. Only drop to 0.5x if the rail leaves you no room to step back.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the bridge along a lower third line, with the river under it and the city beyond.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into early evening is a good bet, when the light is softer and the bridge's lighting starts to show. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your phone on the rail.
card.selfie_here: Try the Station Square end of the bridge, at the steps beside The Grand Concourse, or on the bridge walkway you reach from those steps. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt so the bridge sits over your shoulder. Treat it as a lead: we don't have a confirmed angle, and the walkway has a concrete divider, so the classic couple-in-the-middle shot is tricky.
card.ask_someone: On the trail under the bridge on the Station Square side, ask a passer-by to shoot while you stand in front, so the bridge is overhead in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge is very busy with bikes and walkers, so stand clear of the path when you pose. The Grand View Avenue overlook is on a public street and free to use, but check the official site for closures before you go.
card.challenge: Get the whole span in the shot with the river filling the bottom of the frame, and keep the horizon dead level. No wonky bridges allowed!
card.good_to_know: Gustav Lindenthal designed the bridge, and it opened on 19 March 1883. It's the third bridge on this spot and reuses the stone piers from John A. Roebling's earlier suspension bridge. It was widened in 1889 and 1911, and it's now a National Historic Landmark. A 1994-95 rehabilitation gave it the colourful paint and lighting.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Mount Washington overlook on Grand View Avenue and face the bridge, looking down on it. You want the river and the approach into downtown in the frame too.

card.hook: Deutschtown isn't one big landmark, it's a pile of little scenes: a roofline here, a doorway there, a sign you'd miss if you walked too fast. Think of it as a scavenger hunt with your phone.
card.stand_here: Start near Cedar Avenue: stand about 410 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Then walk towards Deutschtown and take your main photos from the pavement once you're among the buildings.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for a natural view of a single building or corner. Switch to zoom 0.5x in tight spaces to fit in more of the scene and the sky, and use zoom 2x or more to pick out a sign or small detail without stepping into the road.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up a street or building front with them so the verticals stay straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually the most flattering here.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the "Welcome to Deutschtown" mural at the corner of East Ohio Street and Cedar Avenue, at the start of the Deutschtown Neighborhood Trail. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and let the mural fill the frame behind you. Another good backdrop is the Dead & Company mural on the mural side of Allegheny City Brewing.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the sidewalk on the 800 block of Cedar Avenue and shoot with the large late-Victorian houses of the 800 and 900 blocks behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep an eye on traffic and pavements, and be considerate if you photograph people's homes or front doors.
card.challenge: Find three repeating lines, like rooflines, windows and steps, and get them all into one photo.
card.good_to_know: Deutschtown is a neighbourhood, not a single building, so a short, slow walk with your phone ready works better than staying put. The "Welcome to Deutschtown" mural carries the neighbourhood's name and honours its history. If you want to go inside any building, check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start near Cedar Avenue: stand about 410 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Then walk towards Deutschtown and take your main photos from the pavement once you're among the buildings.
